MSK__Joint Pain:
Joint pain (arthralgia) is one of the commonest presenting symptoms — and the trick is a structured sort before you reach for tests. Ask four questions. (1) Articular or periarticular? — is the joint itself painful (pain on all movement, effusion, deep/diffuse) or a tendon / bursa / bone around it (point tenderness, pain on one movement)? (2) Inflammatory or mechanical? — inflammatory = early-morning stiffness >30–60 min, eases with use, swelling / warmth / erythema, night pain, systemic upset; mechanical / degenerative = worse through the day / with use, stiffness <30 min, better with rest. (3) What pattern? — mono (1) vs oligo (2–4) vs poly (≥5), symmetry, large vs small, axial vs peripheral, migratory vs additive (see monoarthritis, polyarthritis). (4) Acute or chronic?
🚨A single acute hot, swollen, painful joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate the joint (before antibiotics if possible) and do not delay (see hot swollen joint, bone & joint infection). Also flagged: fever with systemic upset, joint pain with a rash / photosensitivity, oral ulcers or red eye (connective tissue disease / spondyloarthropathy), new inflammatory arthritis with weight loss or night sweats (malignancy / vasculitis), and any joint pain after trauma (fracture).

1Recognise & sort
🔍Take the pain apart
  • Articular (pain on all movement, effusion) vs periarticular (point tenderness, pain on one specific movement — tendon / bursa)
  • Inflammatory (morning stiffness >30–60 min, eases with use, hot / swollen, night pain) vs mechanical (worse with use, stiffness <30 min, eases with rest)
  • Define onset (acute vs chronic), number of joints, symmetry, and whether it is migratory or additive
🚩Red-flag patterns
  • Single acute hot swollen joint → septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate (see joint infection)
  • Fever / systemic upset, or arthritis with a rash, oral ulcers, red eye or new murmur (CTD, spondyloarthropathy, endocarditis)
  • New inflammatory arthritis + weight loss / night sweats (malignancy / vasculitis); any post-traumatic joint pain (fracture)
🔵Acute patterns
  • Acute monoarthritis: septic arthritis, gout / pseudogout (see crystal arthropathy), haemarthrosis, trauma
  • Migratory (moves joint to joint): gonococcal, rheumatic fever, viral, Lyme, early connective tissue disease
  • Acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis: viral (e.g. parvovirus), early rheumatoid arthritis
🟢Chronic patterns
  • Symmetrical small joints (MCP / PIP / wrist), morning stiffness → rheumatoid arthritis (see RA)
  • Asymmetrical large joints / axial + enthesitis / dactylitis → spondyloarthropathy (psoriatic, reactive, axial, IBD-related, see spondyloarthropathy)
  • DIP + weight-bearing joints, worse with use, bony swelling → osteoarthritis (see OA)
🟣Don’t-miss systemic clues
  • Photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, Raynaud’s, serositis → connective tissue disease / SLE (see CTD)
  • Psoriasis / nail changes, uveitis, urethritis or recent diarrhoea, IBD → a spondyloarthropathy
  • Widespread pain, tender points, fatigue, non-inflammatory → fibromyalgia (a diagnosis of exclusion, see fibromyalgia)
  • Over-50s, proximal shoulder / pelvic-girdle pain + long morning stiffness, very high ESR → polymyalgia rheumatica (watch for giant cell arteritis)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine with look–feel–move: effusion, warmth, deformity, range; screen the other joints, skin, nails and eyes
  • Bloods: FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, RF & anti-CCP, ANA, HLA-B27 (selectively), U&E / LFTs
  • Joint aspiration (MC&S, crystals, Gram — mandatory for a hot joint) and imaging (X-ray, ultrasound / MRI) as guided
Sort before you test. Two questions do most of the work: is it inflammatory or mechanical (the morning-stiffness clock — >30–60 min and easing with use = inflammatory), and how many joints, how symmetrical? Those two axes place most arthritis before a single blood test — and a single hot joint always gets aspirated to exclude sepsis.

MSK__Acute Hot Swollen Joint:
An acute hot, swollen, painful joint is a finding that carries one overriding rule: it is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Untreated septic arthritis destroys the joint within days and carries a real mortality, so the priority is a diagnostic joint aspiration before you commit to any other label. The differential is short and worth knowing cold: septic arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis (trauma / anticoagulation / bleeding disorder), a reactive arthritis, an acute flare of a known inflammatory arthritis, and trauma / fracture. The one test that separates them is the synovial fluid — Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals (see joint pain, bone & joint infection).
🚨Aspirate the joint URGENTLY, before antibiotics — send fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals, take blood cultures, then start empirical IV antibiotics and refer for washout (see septic arthritis). Never dismiss a hot joint as “just a gout flare” — sepsis and crystals can coexist. A prosthetic joint must not be tapped at the bedside — refer to orthopaedics for aspiration in theatre.

1Recognise & act
🔍Recognise it
  • Red, hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint with an effusion, markedly reduced range and held still
  • Ask about fever / systemic upset, speed of onset, prior joint disease, trauma and anticoagulation
  • Note risk factors for sepsis: prosthetic joint, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, immunosuppression, IVDU, a skin breach
🚩The emergency response
  • Septic arthritis until proven otherwise → URGENT aspiration before antibiotics (Gram / culture / crystals / cell count)
  • Take blood cultures + FBC / CRP, then start empirical IV antibiotics and refer for joint washout (see joint infection)
  • Prosthetic joint → do not aspirate at the bedside; refer to orthopaedics for theatre aspiration
🔵The differential
  • Septic arthritis: Staph aureus commonest; gonococcal in the young / sexually active (migratory, tenosynovitis, pustules)
  • Crystal arthritis: gout (podagra, see gouty tophi) and pseudogout (CPPD, knee / wrist, elderly, see crystal arthropathy)
  • Haemarthrosis (trauma, anticoagulation, haemophilia), reactive arthritis, and an acute flare of RA / spondyloarthropathy (see RA)
🟢Read the synovial fluid
  • Septic: turbid / purulent, very high WCC (often >50×10⁹/L, >90% neutrophils), organisms on Gram / culture
  • Crystal: negatively birefringent needles = urate (gout); positively birefringent rhomboids = CPPD (pseudogout)
  • Haemarthrosis: frank blood (± fat globules if intra-articular fracture)
🟣Mimics & pitfalls
  • Cellulitis / bursitis can look similar but the joint moves freely and the effusion is outside the joint line
  • A hot swollen foot in a diabetic may be a Charcot (neuropathic) joint, not infection (see neuropathic foot, Charcot joint)
  • Serum urate is often normal or low during an acute gout attack — it does not exclude gout, and a raised urate does not confirm it
🩺Investigate & treat
  • Joint aspiration (the decisive test) + blood cultures, FBC, CRP / ESR, urate, U&E, coagulation
  • Empirical IV antibiotics after aspiration (per local policy, e.g. flucloxacillin) and surgical washout / drainage
  • In a child with a hot hip use the Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WCC >12) to weigh septic vs transient synovitis
Tap first, label later. Every acute hot swollen joint is septic until the aspirate says otherwise — so the reflex is arthrocentesis before antibiotics, blood cultures, then empirical IV cover and washout. Gout is the commonest true cause, but you can only call it gout after excluding sepsis, because the two can sit in the same joint.

MSK__Monoarthritis:
Monoarthritis is inflammation of a single joint. The first split is tempo. An acute monoarthritis (days) is a medical emergency — septic arthritis until proven otherwise — and is worked up as a hot joint (see acute hot swollen joint): septic, crystal (gout / pseudogout), haemarthrosis, reactive or traumatic. A chronic monoarthritis (persisting >6 weeks) opens a different differential that is easy to forget: osteoarthritis, chronic infection (tuberculosis, fungal, Brucella), a monoarticular presentation of RA / a spondyloarthropathy, pigmented villonodular synovitis, tumour, or avascular necrosis. The unifying move is the same: aspirate the joint — and if it stays undiagnosed, biopsy the synovium (see joint pain).
🚨Any acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate before antibiotics, take blood cultures, and treat (see septic arthritis). Do not be reassured by a “normal” serum urate. For a chronic monoarthritis that resists diagnosis, think tuberculosis and tumour — both need a synovial (or bone) biopsy, not just more blood tests. A hot swollen foot in a diabetic may be a Charcot joint, not sepsis.

  • Osteoarthritis (commonest chronic mono, see OA) and avascular necrosis (see AVN)

  • Imaging (X-ray, ultrasound, MRI); if a chronic mono stays undiagnosed → synovial biopsy (TB, PVNS, tumour)

Acute monoarthritis is a hot-joint emergency (septic until proven otherwise); chronic monoarthritis (>6 weeks) is a different list topped by osteoarthritis, TB and tumour. Both start with a joint aspiration — and the chronic, undiagnosed joint ends with a synovial biopsy.

MSK__Polyarthritis:
Polyarthritis is arthritis of five or more joints (2–4 joints is an oligoarthritis). Unlike a single hot joint, the diagnosis here is made by pattern recognition along a few axes: the symmetry (symmetrical small-joint disease — RA, viral, lupus — versus asymmetrical large-joint ± spinal disease — the spondyloarthropathies), the joint size (small hand joints vs large weight-bearing joints), and the course over time (additive as in RA, migratory / flitting as in rheumatic fever, gonococcus and Lyme, or intermittent as in palindromic rheumatism and gout). Deciding whether the process is inflammatory (early-morning stiffness >30 min, swelling, raised CRP) or non-inflammatory (osteoarthritis) frames everything (see joint pain, monoarthritis).
🚨A polyarthritis is rarely the same emergency as a single hot joint, but do not miss: an acutely septic joint superimposed on a polyarthritis (one joint far angrier than the rest → aspirate it), gonococcal / meningococcal arthritis-dermatitis in the young, and a systemic vasculitis or connective-tissue disease with organ involvement (see vasculitis, connective tissue disease). Early rheumatoid arthritis needs urgent rheumatology referral — a “treat-to-target” window exists before erosions form.

🔍Count & classify
  • ≥5 joints = polyarthritis; 2–4 = oligoarthritis; 1 = monoarthritis (see monoarthritis)

🔵Symmetry & size
  • Symmetrical small joints (MCP / PIP / wrists) → rheumatoid arthritis, viral, lupus
  • Asymmetrical large joints ± spine / DIP → seronegative spondyloarthropathy (see spondyloarthropathy)
  • DIP + Heberden nodes, older, non-inflammatory → osteoarthritis (see OA)
🟢Course over time
  • Additive (joints accumulate and stay) → rheumatoid arthritis (see RA)
  • Migratory / flitting (moves from joint to joint) → rheumatic fever, gonococcal, Lyme (see Lyme disease)
  • Intermittent / self-limiting → palindromic rheumatism, viral, polyarticular gout (see crystal arthropathy)
🟣Look outside the joints
  • Skin: psoriasis, malar / vasculitic rash, tophi, nail pitting; eyes: uveitis, dry eyes; mucosa: ulcers
  • Systemic: fever + salmon rash + sore throat → adult-onset Still’s (see Still's disease); Raynaud’s, sicca → CTD
  • Preceding trigger: sore throat (rheumatic fever), diarrhoea / urethritis (reactive), a viral prodrome (parvovirus B19)
🩺Investigate by pattern
  • Inflammatory markers (CRP / ESR), RF and anti-CCP (RA), ANA → ENA / complement (lupus / CTD)
  • Viral serology (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B / C), urate, HLA-B27 selectively, ASOT if rheumatic fever
  • X-rays of hands / feet (erosions in RA / psoriatic; normal in viral / lupus) — and aspirate any disproportionately hot joint
🚩Don’t-miss patterns
  • One joint far angrier than the rest → superimposed septic arthritis — aspirate it (see joint infection)
  • Young + migratory arthritis + pustules / tenosynovitis → disseminated gonococcus
  • Arthritis + rash + renal / lung / neuro signs → vasculitis or connective-tissue disease — look for organ involvement
Pattern beats the single joint. For many joints, ask four questions — how many, how symmetrical, what size, and what course — and the differential falls out. Symmetrical small-joint + additive is rheumatoid until proven otherwise; asymmetrical large-joint + axial is a spondyloarthropathy; migratory flags rheumatic fever, gonococcus and Lyme.

MSK__Back Pain:
Back pain is one of the commonest presentations in medicine and the great majority is mechanical — benign, movement-related and self-limiting. The entire skill is a triage: sort each patient into mechanical, inflammatory, or “red-flag” serious pathology, and screen actively for the emergencies you cannot miss — cauda equina syndrome, malignancy / metastasis, infection (discitis / epidural abscess), fracture, and a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (see lower back & spine). Alongside these, always remember pain referred from a viscus (aorta, pancreas, kidney, peptic ulcer). Simple mechanical pain does not need imaging; a red flag needs it urgently (see joint pain).
🚨Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency. Saddle anaesthesia, bilateral sciatica, urinary retention with overflow, faecal incontinence or reduced anal tone → immediate whole-spine MRI and surgical decompression — delay causes permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction (see cauda equina / spine). A leaking AAA can present as sudden back pain with collapse — feel for a pulsatile mass (see AAA). Thoracic back pain, night pain and systemic upset should always raise malignancy or infection.

🔍Triage the pattern

🚩Malignancy & infection flags

  • Fracture: osteoporosis, long-term steroids, trauma, sudden pain and a step / focal tenderness (see metabolic bone disease)

MSK__Neck Pain:
Neck pain, like back pain, is usually mechanical — cervical spondylosis, muscular strain or whiplash — and settles with time. The exam skill is the same triage: separate benign mechanical pain from a cervical radiculopathy (nerve root), the can’t-miss cervical myelopathy (spinal-cord compression), and true red-flag pathology — infection, malignancy, fracture and rheumatoid atlanto-axial subluxation. Then remember the neck is a site of referred and dangerous pain: meningitis (meningism, see neck stiffness), cardiac pain to the jaw / neck, and carotid or vertebral artery dissection. The single most important pattern to learn is myelopathy, because it is easily missed and needs surgery (see spinal cord disorders, back pain).
🚨Cervical myelopathy is the neck’s cauda equina. Progressive gait disturbance, clumsy hands, Lhermitte’s phenomenon and upper-motor-neurone signs in the legs (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars, Hoffmann’s) → urgent cervical-spine MRI and spinal referral (see cervical myelopathy). In rheumatoid arthritis, atlanto-axial subluxation can compress the cord — especially dangerous during neck manipulation or intubation (see rheumatoid arthritis). After trauma, immobilise and apply the Canadian C-spine rule; fever + neck stiffness + photophobia is meningitis, not a stiff neck.

MSK__Muscle Weakness:
Muscle weakness means a true loss of power — which must first be separated from its common mimics: pain-limited “weakness” (arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica) and generalised fatigue / asthenia. Once you have true weakness, localise the lesion: is it the muscle (a myopathy — proximal, symmetric, no sensory loss, high CK), the nerve (distal, with sensory signs), the neuromuscular junction (fatigable, ocular / bulbar), or the central / UMN pathway (see weakness — localisation)? This topic follows the myopathy arm — where the key emergencies are inflammatory myositis with breathing / swallowing involvement, an underlying malignancy in dermatomyositis, and rhabdomyolysis.
🚨Rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain + dark urine + very high CK) causes acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia — check CK, U&E and an ECG, and give aggressive IV fluids. Inflammatory myositis that reaches the pharyngeal muscles (dysphagia / aspiration) or the respiratory muscles is an emergency (see inflammatory myositis). Dermatomyositis in an adult is paraneoplastic until proven otherwise — screen for an underlying cancer. A myasthenic crisis (fatigable bulbar / respiratory weakness) needs airway support (see neuromuscular junction disorders).

🔍Is it TRUE weakness?
  • True weakness = reduced power on formal testing; pain-limited effort (arthritis, PMR) and fatigue are the mimics (see PMR / vasculitis)
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica: proximal stiffness & pain, age >50, high ESR, but strength is normal
  • Ask about the functional task: rising from a chair, climbing stairs, combing hair (proximal) vs fine hand tasks / tripping (distal)
🔵Localise the lesion
  • Myopathy (muscle): proximal, symmetric, no sensory loss, reflexes preserved until late, CK raised
  • Neuropathy (nerve): distal, with sensory signs and wasting, reduced reflexes (see foot drop)
  • NMJ: fatigable, ocular / bulbar, no sensory loss, normal CK (myasthenia, see NMJ disorders); UMN / central → see weakness
🟢Causes of a myopathy
  • Inflammatory: polymyositis and dermatomyositis (rash + weakness), inclusion-body myositis (see myositis)
  • Drug / toxic: statins and alcohol (raised CK), long-term steroids (steroid myopathy, typically normal CK); endocrine: thyroid disease, Cushing’s, osteomalacia
  • Inherited: muscular dystrophies (e.g. Duchenne, myotonic) and metabolic myopathies (see muscular dystrophies)
🟣Spot dermatomyositis
  • Heliotrope rash (violaceous lids), Gottron’s papules (knuckles), shawl / V sign, nailfold changes
  • Proximal weakness + these skin signs = dermatomyositis — screen for underlying malignancy in adults
  • Polymyositis is the same weakness without the rash (see connective tissue disease)
🚩Red flags
  • Rhabdomyolysis: muscle pain + dark (tea-coloured) urine + very high CK → AKI + hyperkalaemia; fluids + ECG

  • Myasthenic crisis: worsening fatigable bulbar / respiratory weakness → airway & ITU support (see NMJ)

  • CK (very high in myositis / rhabdomyolysis; mildly raised in many dystrophies but very high in Duchenne / Becker), U&E, TFTs, ESR / CRP, calcium
  • Autoantibodies: ANA, anti-Jo-1 (antisynthetase), anti-Mi-2; EMG and muscle biopsy for inflammatory myopathy
  • Malignancy screen in dermatomyositis; anti-AChR / anti-MuSK antibodies if NMJ suspected

MSK__Bone Pain:
Bone pain arises from the bone itself — a deep, boring, often unremitting ache that is classically worse at night and not simply movement-related (which distinguishes it from joint or muscle pain). The dominant concern is malignancy: in an older adult, metastasis (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid) and myeloma; in a young patient, a primary bone tumour (osteosarcoma, Ewing’s). The rest of the list is metabolic (osteomalacia, Paget’s, hyperparathyroidism), infective (osteomyelitis), traumatic / pathological fracture, avascular necrosis and sickle-cell infarction. Two tools do most of the work: the bone profile (calcium, phosphate, ALP) and a plain X-ray (lytic vs sclerotic).
🚨Bone pain with night pain, rest pain, weight loss or a past cancer is malignancy until proven otherwise. In an older adult think metastasis and myeloma — check calcium (hypercalcaemia), a myeloma screen and PSA, and image (see bone tumours, myeloma). A pathological fracture through abnormal bone, and malignant spinal-cord / cauda equina compression, are the emergencies (see back pain). Fever + focal bone pain is osteomyelitis until proven otherwise (see bone & joint infection).

🔍Recognise bone pain
  • Deep, boring, unremitting ache, often worse at night and not purely movement-related
  • Distinguish from joint pain (see joint pain) and muscle pain; localise to a bone / region and check for a mass or tenderness
  • Ask the malignancy red flags: night / rest pain, weight loss, past cancer, age
🚩Malignancy — the fear
  • Metastasis (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid) — the commonest bone malignancy in adults (see bone tumours)
  • Myeloma: bone pain + hypercalcaemia + renal impairment + anaemia (CRAB), lytic lesions (see myeloma)
  • Primary bone tumour in the young: osteosarcoma (around the knee), Ewing’s — night pain + a mass
🟢Metabolic bone disease
  • Osteomalacia: diffuse bone pain + proximal myopathy, low vitamin D, low Ca / phosphate, high ALP (see muscle weakness)
  • Paget’s disease: bone pain, deformity / warmth, isolated very high ALP with normal calcium (see metabolic bone disease)
  • Hyperparathyroidism: high Ca, bone pain (“stones, bones, groans”), osteitis fibrosa cystica
🟣Infection, fracture & infarct
  • Osteomyelitis: fever + focal bone pain / tenderness; Staph aureus, or Salmonella in sickle cell (see bone infection)
  • Fracture: traumatic, stress (athlete), or pathological through tumour / osteoporotic bone
  • Avascular necrosis (see AVN) and sickle-cell bone infarction / crisis
🩺Read the bone profile
  • High ALP + normal Ca + deformity / warmth → Paget’s; high ALP + low Ca / phosphate + myopathy → osteomalacia
  • High calcium + bone pain → myeloma, bony metastasis or hyperparathyroidism
  • Remember osteoporosis is painless until it fractures — pain means a fracture or another diagnosis
🩺Investigate
  • Bone profile (Ca, phosphate, ALP), PTH, vitamin D, FBC / ESR, PSA, myeloma screen (electrophoresis / light chains)
  • Plain X-ray (lytic vs sclerotic, periosteal reaction); isotope bone scan for metastases; MRI for cord / marrow / primary tumour
  • Biopsy any suspected primary bone tumour at a specialist centre — a badly-placed biopsy compromises limb salvage

A deep, night-time bone ache in an older adult means metastasis or myeloma until the calcium, myeloma screen, PSA and X-ray say otherwise; in a young patient with night pain and a mass, think primary bone tumour. Confirm it is bone pain (deep, boring, night); localise it; and screen the malignancy red flags (night / rest pain, weight loss, past cancer)
Examine
Local tenderness, mass, deformity, warmth; check for a primary cancer (breast, prostate, thyroid, chest) and for pathological-fracture risk
Bloods
Bone profile (Ca, phosphate, ALP), PTH, vitamin D, FBC / ESR, PSA, myeloma screen; renal function
Imaging & biopsy
Plain X-ray first; isotope bone scan for metastases, MRI for cord / marrow / primary; biopsy a suspected primary at a specialist sarcoma centre

The rules that carry it: bone pain is deep, boring and worse at night, and malignant until proven otherwise — screen for metastasis and myeloma (calcium, myeloma screen, PSA, X-ray) and, in the young, a primary bone tumour. The bone profile sorts Paget’s (isolated high ALP) from osteomalacia from hypercalcaemic causes; biopsy primaries at a specialist centre.

MSK__Limp / Difficulty Walking:
A limp is an asymmetric, abnormal gait — usually from pain (an antalgic gait, with a shortened stance phase on the sore leg), weakness (a Trendelenburg gait from weak hip abductors) or deformity / limb-length. The exam skill is the child: a limp in a child is worked up by age, and the one diagnosis you can never miss is septic arthritis. Structure it — 0–4 years (DDH, toddler’s fracture, non-accidental injury), 4–10 years (transient synovitis, the commonest, and Perthes), and 10–16 years (SUFE) — but septic arthritis, malignancy and NAI occur at any age (see paediatric orthopaedics, gait patterns).
🚨A child who is febrile and will not weight-bear has septic arthritis until proven otherwise — use the Kocher criteria and aspirate the joint (see septic arthritis, acute hot joint). In an adolescent, hip, thigh OR knee pain with a limp is a SUFE until excluded — always examine the hip in a child with knee pain. Beware non-accidental injury (inconsistent history, other injuries; see safeguarding) and malignancy (leukaemia) with systemic features (see paediatric cancers).

1Characterise & age-sort
🔍Characterise the gait
  • Antalgic (painful): shortened stance phase on the affected leg — points to a painful cause
  • Trendelenburg (pelvis drops to the opposite side on standing on the affected leg): weak hip abductors / hip pathology
  • Then screen for fever, systemic upset, trauma and the child’s age (see gait abnormalities)
🚩Always exclude septic arthritis
  • Febrile, will not weight-bear, holds the joint still, very tender → septic arthritis (see joint infection)
  • Kocher criteria: non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WCC >12 — more met = higher risk
  • Aspirate the joint and treat — the alternative (transient synovitis) is a diagnosis of exclusion
🟢Age 0–4 & 4–10
  • 0–4: DDH (waddling / limp, missed on screening), toddler’s fracture, non-accidental injury
  • 4–10: transient synovitis (post-viral, well / afebrile, weight-bears with a limp) — the commonest
  • Perthes (boys 4–8): avascular necrosis of the femoral head, insidious limp, reduced abduction / internal rotation (see paediatric orthopaedics)
🚩Age 10–16 — SUFE
  • Slipped upper femoral epiphysis: obese adolescent, often around the growth spurt; hip / thigh / knee pain
  • The leg lies externally rotated and shortened, with loss of internal rotation; confirm on a frog-leg lateral X-ray
  • Examine the hip in any child with knee pain — SUFE risks avascular necrosis and needs surgical pinning
🟣Don’t-miss & systemic
  • Non-accidental injury: inconsistent / changing history, delayed presentation, other bruises / fractures (see safeguarding)
  • Malignancy (leukaemia): night pain, pallor, bruising, hepatosplenomegaly, systemic upset (see paediatric cancers)
  • JIA: persistent arthritis >6 weeks, morning stiffness, a swollen joint (see JIA)
🩺Adults & investigation
  • Adult limp: osteoarthritis (hip / knee, see OA), fracture, lumbar radiculopathy, foot pathology, inflammatory arthritis
  • Child: FBC, CRP / ESR, blood cultures, X-ray (both hips, frog-leg for SUFE), ultrasound hip (effusion), and aspiration if septic
  • Apply Kocher to septic-vs-transient; a well, afebrile, weight-bearing child with normal bloods can often be observed
Age structures the child’s limp — but septic arthritis is timeless. Sort by age (0–4 DDH / NAI, 4–10 transient synovitis / Perthes, 10–16 SUFE), yet in every age a febrile, non-weight-bearing child is septic arthritis until the Kocher criteria and an aspirate say otherwise. And knee pain in a child is a hip until proven otherwise.

Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion. A well, afebrile child who weight-bears with a limp after a viral illness, with normal inflammatory markers, likely has transient synovitis — but you reach it only after the Kocher criteria and clinical picture have excluded septic arthritis. If in doubt, aspirate.

FBC, CRP / ESR, blood cultures; X-ray (both hips + frog-leg lateral), hip ultrasound for effusion; apply the Kocher criteria

Septic arthritis → aspirate + antibiotics + washout; SUFE → non-weight-bear + urgent ortho (pinning); NAI / malignancy → safeguard / haematology
